lesson.title: Reading the Skew: What the Gap Between Mean and Median Tells You
lesson.summary: The relationship between the mean and the median reveals the shape of a distribution: they are close together for roughly symmetric data, the mean is pulled above the median in right skewed data, and the mean is pulled below the median in left skewed data.
lesson.body:
Once you know that the mean is pulled toward extreme values while the median resists that pull, you already have the tool you need to diagnose the shape of a distribution without even looking at a graph. In a distribution that is roughly symmetric, the values above the center balance out the values below it, so the mean and the median land close to the same place. In a skewed distribution, one tail stretches farther than the other, and that stretched tail pulls the mean along with it while leaving the median largely undisturbed.

The rule is direction based. In a right skewed distribution, the longer tail points toward larger values, so a handful of unusually large observations drag the mean upward while the median stays anchored near the bulk of the data; this gives the pattern mean greater than median. In a left skewed distribution, the longer tail points toward smaller values, a few unusually small observations pull the mean downward, and the median stays higher; this gives the pattern mean less than median. When neither tail dominates, mean and median are approximately equal, which is one signal, though not the only one, of a symmetric shape.

Suppose eight students report the number of hours they spent on a project: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, and 20 hours, with one student who worked far longer than everyone else. The sum of these values is 45, so the mean is 45 divided by 8, or 5.625 hours. The median, the average of the fourth and fifth sorted values, 4 and 4, is exactly 4 hours. The mean sits noticeably above the median, 5.625 versus 4, and that gap is the signature of right skew: the single large value of 20 hours stretched the right tail and pulled the mean up while the median stayed anchored where most students actually landed.

This comparison is more than a classroom trick; it is often the fastest way to describe a distribution's shape from summary statistics alone, without ever seeing the raw data or a histogram. If a report tells you that the mean home price in a city is well above the median home price, you can immediately infer a right skewed market with some very expensive homes pulling the average up. If a report tells you that a group's mean test score is below its median, you can infer a left skewed distribution, likely caused by one or more unusually low scores.

Keep in mind that this comparison is a useful signal, not an absolute proof of shape. It is possible, though less common, for a distribution to be skewed without a large mean median gap, or for a small data set to produce a gap purely by chance. Still, checking whether the mean sits above, below, or right at the median is almost always your first, fastest step in describing a distribution, and it sets up the more detailed measures of spread that come next, including the range and the standard deviation.
